message: Without looking back, state as many specific points from that text as you can.
response:
These are from memory, and I'll mark where I'm unsure. The note itself warns that recollection drifts, so they should be checked against the text before anyone relies on them.

## Framing

- The title is "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team."
- It is about working with the material the team uses and with the people around you.
- It is short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It is written down because good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a confident colleague is in the room.

## 1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned

- Every claim, whether from a paper, a colleague, a summary or your own earlier notes, has earned a weight from its evidence. Hold it at exactly that weight.
- Not more because it is fluent, comes from someone senior, or confirms what you hoped.
- Not less because it is inconvenient, comes from someone junior, or because doubting feels rigorous.
- Ask what supports it, how directly, and what would have to be true for it to be wrong.
- A well-measured result from a controlled comparison is heavy.
- A mechanism suggested after the data came in is light but not nothing. Note it and say what would test it.
- Confidence is information about the speaker, not about the world.
- Inflation is easy to spot afterwards. Deflation is harder: a caveat on a sound result looks careful but is a misreport.
- Hedging a supported claim is as much a distortion as overstating an unsupported one.
- **Example:** a supplier's defect rate fell after a process change. If the evidence is three months of the supplier's own figures, say so. If it is a year of your own incoming inspection, don't bury it under "it may be noise."

## 2. Take in what was said before you answer

- Before responding, take in all of it and show that you have by restating the substance briefly in your own terms.
- This is not politeness. It is how both sides find out whether what was received matches what was sent.
- The part you don't restate is the part most likely to drop.
- A reply that handles the three easy points and silently skips the hard fourth has answered a different, easier message.
- If you can't restate something, you haven't understood it, and the next move is a question.
- Then move on. Restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful part is the implication, the gap or the next test.
- **Example:** a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. You restate all five in a line each, answer four, and say plainly that the budget needs figures you don't yet have and when you will.

## 3. Go to the source

- Summaries, abstracts, notes and memory are compressions. Compression loses exactly what later matters: the denominator, the subgroup, the condition under which a result held.
- When a decision depends on a specific detail, check the primary material.
- This applies most to things you think you already know. Claims repeated many times are the most likely to have drifted.
- The source is the referee, not agreement among colleagues.
- A team that checks claims against each other rather than the data can drift together into a shared mistake that no one inside it can see.
- **Example:** you remember "costs fell 12%," but the report said cost per unit fell 12% while volume fell 20%. Open it before citing it in a budget meeting.

## 4. Don't close what is open, and don't keep open what is closed

- Mark honestly which questions the evidence settles and which it leaves open.
- Closing early feels like progress but turns uncertainty into a false fact that others build on. If something is open, say so and say what would close it.
- The mirror failure is keeping a settled question open out of discomfort, or because one more check feels safer. That wastes effort and signals doubt the evidence doesn't support.
- **Example:** a new form reduces errors at two sites, and whether it works at the busiest site, with a different workflow, is open. Report the first as found and the second as open, not "promising" and "likely."

## 5. Value the colleague who sees differently

- The most useful thing a colleague offers is what you couldn't produce yourself: an objection from a different starting point.
- A reviewer who knows what you know mostly hands back what you already see. Difference is the source of new information.
- When asking for a check, give the material and the question, not your conclusion, your worries or what you hope they'll find. Sharing your view removes the difference that made them worth asking.
- In reverse: when you are the fresh reader, read first, form your view, then look at others' conclusions.
- Raise objections when you have them. One held back because the room seems settled is information the team never gets.

## 6. Make your moves where they can be seen

- When you can see the right next step, take it, and make it visible so others can check or reverse it.
- Share drafts before they feel finished, make the call and show your reasoning, and push results out so someone can look.
- Asking permission for something the evidence settles hands the decision to someone with less context and stalls the work on your guess about what they would say.
- That guess is your own model of them and contains nothing new. Only a real move gets a real reply.
- This is not licence to ignore others. Moves that are hard to reverse or commit other people's time deserve a conversation first. Most moves are reversible, and the default for those is to make them openly.
- **Example:** rather than asking whether to restructure section three, restructure it in a copy, say what changed and why, and invite reversal.

## 7. Failures come in pairs

- Inflating a claim / deflating it.
- Inventing a flaw to look rigorous / inventing a reassurance to keep things moving.
- Closing too early / keeping open too long.
- Killing a live line at the first difficulty / keeping a dead one the evidence has ruled out.
- Deferring to a claim because of who made it / dismissing it for the same reason.
- Offloading decisions you can see / overriding where others' input is genuinely needed.
- If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.

## A last word

- It is not a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and you will mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the work itself: the source that overrules you, the colleague who reads differently, the result that doesn't come out as expected.
- Welcome those, because they are how you learn what you didn't already know.

## Confidence

- **Sections 1 to 4 and 7:** high, including the examples and the list of pairs. The exact wording of the pairs may differ slightly.
- **Section 5:** I recall no worked example, though I'm less sure of that than of the rest.
- **The last word:** the gist is right, but my phrasing is probably closer to a paraphrase than in the other sections.
